bottomCallout: Mercedes-Benz VAN Program · Kromberg & Schubert, Kenitra (Plant K3)
speaker: Wijdane & Salma
speakerNotes: Good morning. We are Wijdane Laaguidi and Salma Lsilis. Our research began inside the Logistics Department of Kromberg & Schubert in Kenitra, during the pre-series phase of the Mercedes-Benz VAN program. It starts with something we saw, not something we assumed.

title: We entered the supply chain from the inside: Procurement and Planning, side by side

cards.title: K&S Group
cards.description: German company founded in 1902, headquartered in Abensberg; 50,000+ people, 40+ sites

cards.title: Kenitra, Morocco
cards.description: First plant K1 opened in 2015; Plant K3 runs the Mercedes-Benz VAN program

cards.title: Logistics Department
cards.description: Disposition (Procurement) · Planning · Material Flow · Incoming · Dispatch · Transport

cards.title: Our seats in the system
cards.description: Wijdane: Raw Material Procurement · Salma: Production Planning

bottomCallout: Research context: pre-series production at K3, with the transition to mass production expected about two weeks after the study window — a real industrial situation, not an abstract assumption.
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: Our internship was the starting point of the research. We were embedded in the Logistics Department at Plant K3 — Wijdane in Raw Material Procurement, Salma in Production Planning — so we saw the same demand flow from two sides. The study took place during pre-series, shortly before mass production.

title: From pre-series to mass production: the window to fix coordination before volumes rise
subtitle: PRE-SERIES

cards.title: PRE-SERIES
cards.description:
Capacity and output still developing
Requirements and technical modifications keep changing
Readiness depends on supplier quality and deliveries

cards.title: TRANSITION
cards.description:
Mass production expected about two weeks after the study window
Coordination routines must exist before volumes increase
Escalation and MOCA practices still improvised

cards.title: MASS PRODUCTION
cards.description:
External cover (Macedonia, K2) phased out
No documented replacement capacity or contingency plan yet
Needs stable, shared coordination

bottomCallout: Pre-series is the opportunity to identify and correct coordination weaknesses before volumes increase
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: Pre-series is not a small version of mass production: capacity is still developing and requirements keep changing. The transition therefore matters — and it is also when the external cover from Macedonia and K2 is phased out. We make no claim on the plant’s production performance; this is the context.

title: EDI transmits the customer’s changes — but who acts on them?
subtitle: CUSTOMER

cards.title: Mercedes-Benz EDI
cards.description: 14-day contractual lead time. Call-offs and revisions: ↑ ↓ postponed · cancelled

cards.title: Production Planning
cards.description: Receives and interprets the change — determines what must change, where, by when

cards.title: Operational Decisions
cards.description: Procurement & purchase commitments · Material availability · Scheduling · Capacity · IE · Material Flow

bulletPoints: 1. Transmission (EDI solves this only)
2. Interpretation
3. Decision
4. Coordination
5. Execution & follow-up
bottomCallout: EDI transmits customer information — but receiving it does not automatically guarantee coordinated operational action
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: EDI is how Mercedes-Benz sends call-offs and revisions: quantities can go up, down, be postponed or cancelled. Planning receives them first, but each revision touches procurement, material availability, scheduling, capacity, engineering and material flow at once. EDI covers only the first step: transmission.

title: The first warning signs: the same demand change, felt differently across functions
subtitle: Mercedes-Benz EDI

cards.title: Type 1 vs Type 2/3 Orders
cards.description: Type 1 changes update automatically; Type 2/3 are re-entered manually, so information arrives late

cards.title: Spreadsheet Coordination
cards.description: Coordination relies on emails and spreadsheets; a duplicated requirement file nearly triggered unwarranted purchases

cards.title: Indirect Material Alert
cards.description: Material Flow often learns of an increase when the shop floor runs out of wires

cards.title: Lateral Friction
cards.description: Quality blocked substitute wires until IE finalized the AVI document. Planning and IE disagree: uniform standard time vs harness-specific times

bottomCallout: We saw it first; Act II tests whether it was systematic
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: These are observations and practitioner accounts, not yet conclusions. Type 1 changes update automatically, Type 2 and 3 are re-entered by hand; coordination ran on emails and spreadsheets; Material Flow often learned of increases only when the shop floor ran out of wire. Two lateral frictions also appeared. Did this happen once, or was it systematic?

title: The gap: information arrives, but coordinated action does not follow automatically
subtitle: INITIAL OBSERVATION
bulletPoints: INITIAL OBSERVATION:
Changes reached functions at different times, and sometimes only after consequences were visible.
Impacted Functions: Procurement, Material Flow, Capacity, Industrial Engineering, Production.
secondaryColumn: POTENTIAL OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCES:
• Shortage on critical components
• Backlog accumulation on shop floor
• Capacity pressure and unplanned overtime
• Excess stock in warehouse
• Material obsolescence exposure
bottomCallout: A coordination gap, not a knowledge gap: the steps are known, but no owner, timeline or shared procedure exists
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: On the left, what we first noticed. On the right, what the investigation established: all four departments knew the escalation steps. So this is a coordination gap, not a knowledge gap. The centre diagram shows where the gap sits — between receiving the change and acting across functions.

title: Problem statement and research questions

cards.title: Interdependent Impact
cards.description: Each EDI revision hits several interdependent activities at once. Updates do not reach all functions simultaneously.

cards.title: Escalation Ladder
cards.description: How are demand increases handled?

cards.title: MOCA / Obsolescence
cards.description: How are demand decreases handled?

cards.title: Coordination
cards.description: How does information flow between functions?

bottomCallout: Risk: shortages, backlog, excess stock and obsolescence, sharpest in the move to mass production.
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: The problem is not demand variability alone, but how its consequences are communicated and managed across functions. Our main question asks how Procurement, Planning and Capacity Management can be better coordinated. The three supporting questions look at the escalation ladder, MOCA and obsolescence, and cross-functional coordination.

title: From observation to a structured research project
subtitle: OBSERVE

cards.title: Cross-Functional Coordination
cards.description: Identify operational and organizational difficulties of EDI demand changes and propose an integrated approach to cross-functional coordination

cards.title: Mechanisms & Linkages
cards.description: Understand how increases and decreases affect decisions · identify coordination difficulties · connect demand information with materials, suppliers, schedules and capacity

cards.title: Academic & Practical
cards.description:
Academic: a context-specific coordination framework for pre-series to mass production.
Practical: a structured model for cross-functional decisions at K&S

bottomCallout: OBSERVE → IDENTIFY → INVESTIGATE → ANALYSE → DEVELOP A MODEL
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: We moved from observing to a structured investigation. The aim was never only to describe demand variability; it was to understand its consequences and build a structured coordination approach. Academic contribution: a context-specific framework; practical contribution: the ISCC Model.

title: Constructivism, mixed methods and an action-research logic
subtitle: PARADIGM

cards.title: Constructivism
cards.description: Meaning is built through practitioners’ interpretation: Planning and Procurement read the same EDI change differently

cards.title: Constructive Research Approach
cards.description: Embedded single-case study: K&S, Mercedes-Benz VAN program

cards.title: Mixed Methods
cards.description: Qualitative and quantitative evidence combined, not run in parallel

cards.title: Action-Research Logic
cards.description: Diagnose, build a provisional model, refine with practitioners; agreement is not proof of improvement

bottomCallout: TRIANGULATION: Interviews + Observations + Company records (Excel, ERP/Krosy) — comparing sources to strengthen credibility
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: These are four different things and we keep them distinct. Constructivism is the epistemological paradigm. The design is a constructive research approach with an embedded single case. Mixed methods is how evidence is combined. Action-research logic is the diagnose, model, refine loop. Triangulation supports credibility. Practitioner agreement is not proof of improvement.

title: Two evidence streams: ten voices and the company’s own records
subtitle: QUALITATIVE
bulletPoints: QUALITATIVE STREAM (10 Interviews):
• Purposive sample across all key functions
• Experience ranging from ~1.5 to 14 years
• Interview guide adapted to each function
• Field notes: daily replanning, procurement escalation meetings
secondaryColumn: QUANTITATIVE STREAM (Company Records):
• EDI call-off overviews: demand variability (Release CW28 vs CW29)
• Excel weekly plans & requirement lists: LAB vs VSAT
• ERP/Krosy reports: backlog and material coverage checks
bottomCallout: Qualitative + quantitative evidence → TRIANGULATION → a fuller understanding of the coordination problem
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: Qualitative: ten semi-structured interviews, chosen purposively across Planning, Procurement, Industrial Engineering, Material Flow and Production Management, plus field observation. Quantitative: existing operational records — EDI call-off overviews, Excel production plans and requirement lists, and ERP/Krosy reports. Combined, they triangulate.

title: What the professionals revealed: five recurring themes
subtitle: Improvised escalation

cards.title: Improvised Escalation
cards.description: All four departments confirm the ladder exists, yet no owner or fixed timeline

cards.title: Uneven Information
cards.description: Type 2/3 changes re-entered by hand; emails and spreadsheets; Material Flow learns indirectly

cards.title: Supplier Rigidity
cards.description: Frozen weeks: 0% increase in weeks 0–2, then 20%; one single-source freeze ≈ 70% of shortage impact

cards.title: Capacity & Friction
cards.description: Up to +20% absorbed; above it: overtime, weekends. Quality ↔ IE (AVI document) & Planning ↔ IE resolved informally

bottomCallout: IN THEIR WORDS: "improvised each time" (Procurement) · "logical, but improvised" (Material Flow) · "lack of information" (Material Flow)
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: Organized by theme rather than department. Every department described escalation as improvised. Information moves unevenly by order type and channel. Suppliers enforce frozen weeks and one single-source freeze drove about 70% of shortage impact. Above a 20% increase, capacity needs extra measures. And frictions run laterally, not only Planning to Procurement.

title: Measuring the problem: demand moves almost every week

metrics.label: Largest Single-Week Drop
metrics.sublabel: Units in CW34; fell to 0 in CW30–CW35

bottomCallout: CW35 (9,723.3%) is a calculation artifact (86 LAB vs 8,362 VSAT units) and is excluded.
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: The problem is measurable, not only an impression. Between the CW28 and CW29 releases, 54 of 59 weeks changed, with average variation of 44.1% against a 20% internal flexibility window. Near-term call-offs fell to zero in CW30 to CW35. In CW40, 110,671 units were required against 24,758 confirmed. CW35 is a calculation artifact and is excluded.

title: What the combined evidence confirmed
subtitle: UNEXPECTED RESULTS

rows: Sudden changes are complex and non-standardized (Planning)
54 of 59 weeks changed; average variation 44.1% vs 20% window
All four departments: no formal owner or timeline
Sister plant ~24 h, Planning ~1 day, IE 1–2 days, freight up to 2 weeks vs 14-day lead time
A coordination gap, not a knowledge gap
MOCA first, then scrap via CMT; one case split 75% / 25%
Call-offs fell to 0 in CW30–CW35 (−505 in CW34)
Obsolescence exposure when decreases follow commitments
Planning negotiates weekend work and rebalancing
Capacity pressure; the gap is not only planning inaccuracy

bottomCallout: UNEXPECTED RESULTS: Type 2/3 orders delay information · Written guidelines, yet universal improvisation · Difficulty depends on role · Pre-series cover is temporary · Friction beyond Planning–Procurement
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: Read each row left to right: what we observed, what practitioners said, what the records show, and our interpretation. The strength comes from the evidence, and we do not claim EDI variability alone causes every consequence. Beneath are the five results that surprised us.

title: Why the gap matters: increases and decreases hurt differently
subtitle: DEMAND INCREASES
bulletPoints: DEMAND INCREASES (↑):
• Escalation ladder: sister plant (~24 h) → Planning (~1 day) → IE (1–2 days) → special freight (up to 2 weeks)
• Suppliers: 0% increase in weeks 0–2, then +20%
• Above +20%: extra operators, workstations, overtime, weekends
• Pre-series cover from Macedonia and K2 is being phased out
secondaryColumn: DEMAND DECREASES (↓):
• MOCA first: redistribute surplus to sister plants
• Otherwise scrap, allocated via CMT: customer-driven vs internal over-ordering (one case: 75% / 25%)
• Suppliers allow 0% reduction in the earliest weeks
• MOCA is triggered only after the excess stock has arrived
bottomCallout: The response is cross-functional: Planning · Procurement · Industrial Engineering · Material Flow · Quality
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: The two directions create different problems, so the response cannot sit in Planning alone. Increases push on suppliers, capacity and emergency measures. Decreases expose existing purchase commitments and surplus stock. Procurement and Material Flow find decreases easier; Planning finds increases harder; IE finds both equally demanding.

title: Three lenses on the same problem

cards.title: Lawrence & Lorsch (1967)
cards.description: No single best structure: coordination must fit the environment and its uncertainty. So: different responses to increases and decreases

cards.title: Teece, Pisano & Shuen (1997)
cards.description: Sensing → Seizing → Transforming: detect change, act on it, renew routines. So: detect, decide and adapt, not just react

cards.title: Masudin & Kamara (2017); Tao et al. (2025)
cards.description: EDI is an enabler; value depends on turning information into coordinated action. So: align information, responsibilities and decisions

bottomCallout: Context: ramp-up and pre-series logistics require coordinated capacity, materials and information flows before series production
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: We used theory to interpret what we found, not to decorate. Contingency Theory explains why responses must fit the situation. Dynamic Capabilities explains how an organization senses, seizes and transforms. Supply Chain Integration explains why EDI is an enabler, not a solution. Ramp-up literature sets the context.

title: From theory to the K&S case
subtitle: Theory interprets the real problem; it does not replace the evidence

rows: Fit the coordination response to the conditions and uncertainty
Separate responses for increases and decreases; the 20% capacity threshold; role-dependent difficulty
How an organization detects change, acts and renews its routines
Sense: Type 2/3 changes arrive late. Seize: escalation executed informally. Transform: give the ladder and MOCA owners and timelines
EDI enables information exchange; integration needs aligned decisions
Common planning reference for Planning, Procurement, IE, Material Flow and Quality, not only Planning–Procurement

bottomCallout: Theory interprets the real problem; it does not replace the evidence
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: Each theory answers a question the evidence raised. Contingency Theory: why treat increases and decreases differently. Dynamic Capabilities: where K&S senses late, seizes informally and has not yet transformed its routines. Supply Chain Integration: why fixing Planning to Procurement alone is not enough.

title: Why we built the ISCC Model
subtitle: Identified gap

cards.title: Coordination Gap
cards.description: Information received via EDI, but no coordinated cross-functional response follows automatically

cards.title: Field Evidence
cards.description: Improvised execution · Type 2/3 delay · lateral friction · two directions of risk (shortage vs obsolescence)

cards.title: Academic Anchors
cards.description: Contingency Theory · Dynamic Capabilities · Supply Chain Integration

cards.title: Weaknesses Addressed
cards.description:
1. No ownership of each step
2. No defined response times
3. Delayed, manual information
4. No shared record of decisions

bottomCallout: ISCC = Integrated Supply-Chain Coordination — closing the 4 structural weaknesses before mass production
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: The model is a response to the actual problem. Three inputs: the identified gap, the empirical findings and the theoretical foundations. It builds on the escalation ladder and MOCA rather than replacing them, and it treats increases and decreases within one coordination structure.

title: The ISCC Model: from EDI information to coordinated decisions
subtitle: Stage 1 – EDI Demand Variability
bulletPoints: ISCC 5-STAGE FRAMEWORK:
• Stage 1 – EDI Demand Variability: Changes in customer demand and component requirements
• Stage 2 – Information & Coordination Requirements: Interpretation, communication, assessment and sharing
• Stage 3 – Cross-functional Operational Planning: Procurement · Production planning · Capacity management
• Stage 4A – Demand Increase: Material shortage, capacity pressure, backlog risk
• Stage 4B – Demand Decrease: Excess raw materials, inventory exposure, obsolescence risk
• Stage 5 – Integrated Supply-Chain Coordination: Coordinated decisions across functions
secondaryColumn: LINKS TO K&S PRACTICE:
• Stage 2: Automatic notification of Type 2/3 changes
• Stage 4A: Formalize the Escalation Ladder (owners & strict time limits)
• Stage 4B: Trigger MOCA and CMT review earlier at call-off drop
• Stage 5: Maintain a shared decision record across departments
bottomCallout: Builds on existing mechanisms; not yet implemented or validated.
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: This is the model as presented in the thesis: five stages. Stage 1, EDI demand variability. Stage 2, how changes are interpreted, communicated and assessed. Stage 3, Procurement, Planning and Capacity linked. Stage 4A, increase risks; 4B, decrease risks. Stage 5, coordinated decisions. It is a provisional, practitioner-informed model, not yet validated by implementation.

title: How the ISCC Model can prepare the move to mass production
subtitle: IDENTIFIED CHALLENGE

rows: Predictable response within the 14-day lead time
MOCA review triggered at the call-off drop
External cover phased out, no contingency plan

bottomCallout: Preparing Plant K3 for mass production readiness as external cover from Macedonia/K2 phases out
speaker: Salma Lsilis
speakerNotes: This slide separates what was found from what is expected. The left column is documented. The middle column is the proposed ISCC approach. The right column is expected benefit only: the thesis proposes the model and does not show measured improvements from implementation.

act: ACT VI · FROM FINDINGS TO ACTION
title: Recommendations and implementation priorities
subtitle: Priority = relevance to the findings and feasibility: formalize existing mechanisms first

rows: Assign an owner and time limit to each escalation step; keep a common decision record
Predictable response inside the 14-day lead time
Extend automatic notifications to Type 2/3 order changes
Trigger the MOCA review at the call-off drop; keep Planning and IE involved in decreases
Agree a shared procedure for cross-functional disagreements (AVI release, standard times)
Document contingency capacity for the end of Macedonia/K2 cover

bottomCallout: Priority = relevance to the findings and feasibility: formalize existing mechanisms first
speaker: Wijdane Laaguidi
speakerNotes: Recommendations follow the findings. Priority one formalizes what already exists, which is the most feasible. Priority two extends automatic notification. Rows three and five are our proposals derived from the findings; the priority order reflects relevance and feasibility.

act: ACT VI · FROM FINDINGS TO ACTION
title: Limitations and conclusion
subtitle: Single case
bulletPoints: LIMITATIONS:
• Single case: One plant (K3), one OEM program (Mercedes-Benz VAN)
• Interview depth: Several IE answers recorded as "same as first"
• Uneven coverage: Not every role answered every question
• Short window: ~2 weeks to mass production; model not observed after implementation
secondaryColumn: CONCLUSION:
1. Problem: EDI changes reach functions unevenly: a coordination gap
2. Evidence: Changes in 54 of 59 weeks; improvised escalation; lateral friction
3. Contribution: The ISCC Model, grounded in evidence and theory
4. Why now: Coordination must be structured before mass production
bottomCallout: A grounded, empirical contribution ready for implementation before series production ramp-up
speaker: Wijdane & Salma
speakerNotes: The limits are honest ones: a single case, uneven interview depth, uneven question coverage, and a short window with no post-implementation observation. Our conclusion: we observed a real coordination gap, measured and explained it, interpreted it theoretically, and proposed the ISCC Model to close it before mass production.
